final_proof:
Let \(V=\mathbb F^n\), and regard \(A\) and \(B\) as linear maps \(V\to V\) acting on column vectors. We first suppose that \(B\) is a left inverse of \(A\), so that \(BA=I_n\). If \(x\in\ker A\), then
\[
x=I_nx=(BA)x=B(Ax)=0.
\]
Thus \(A\) is injective. To see explicitly why this implies surjectivity here, let \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\) be the standard basis of \(V\). The vectors \(Ae_1,\ldots,Ae_n\) are linearly independent: if
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n c_iAe_i=0,
\]
then \(A(\sum_{i=1}^n c_ie_i)=0\), and injectivity of \(A\) gives \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_ie_i=0\), whence every \(c_i=0\). Since \(V\) has dimension \(n\), these \(n\) linearly independent vectors form a basis of \(V\). Consequently, \(A\) is surjective.

Now take any \(y\in V\). By surjectivity, there is an \(x\in V\) such that \(y=Ax\). Therefore
\[
(AB)y=AB(Ax)=A(BA)x=AI_nx=Ax=y.
\]
Hence \(AB\) acts as the identity on every vector in \(V\), so \(AB=I_n\). Therefore every left inverse \(B\) of the square matrix \(A\) is also a right inverse.

Conversely, suppose that \(B\) is a right inverse of \(A\), so \(AB=I_n\). Then \(A\) is a left inverse of \(B\). Applying the result just proved with \(B\) in place of \(A\) and \(A\) in place of \(B\) yields \(BA=I_n\). Thus every right inverse of a square matrix is also a left inverse. (The problem's last sentence says “right inverse” twice; taken literally, that sentence is immediate, while the preceding argument proves the evidently intended converse.)

In particular, left and right inverses are equal whenever they are initially presented separately: if \(LA=I_n\) and \(AR=I_n\), then
\[
L=LI_n=L(AR)=(LA)R=I_nR=R.
\]
This also proves the assertion expressed in the title.
